nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Product life-cycle analysis|Disposal methods_qna_000
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What is the current status of municipal landfills regarding the disposal of POPs in high-income countries?
nodes.answer: Many high-income countries have disposed of POPs containing municipal waste in landfills, and countries like Australia, New Zealand, and the US still do so due to limited waste destruction capacity.
nodes.paragraph: Also, many high income countries have disposed POPs containing municipal waste largely in landfills until recently and some coun tries, such as Australia, New Zealand, and the US with limited waste destruction capacity, still dispose POPs containing waste to landfills [46, 167, 184, 189, 362]. Therefore, municipal landfills are joining chemical landfills as reservoirs of POPs and other PBTs albeit at a lower pollution inventory for individual sites, but they represent a large overall inventory considering the hundreds of thousands of landfills including those that predate modern environmental regulations, and which do not have lining and caping systems and waste is not isolated from the surrounding environment [29]. Whilst in the frame of the Stockholm Convention POPs inventories are developed, e.g., for polychlorin ated biphenyls (PCBs) in transformers and capaci tors or PBDEs in electronic waste, the POPs disposed to landfills or in contaminated sites are normally not quantified with some exemptions like large pesticide landfills [234, 294, 349, 351]. Inventories of uninten tionally produced POPs, such as PCDD/PCDF, are largely developed as release inventories for specific years [86, 354] and mostly do not consider the historic reservoirs and releases with a few exemptions [198, 289, 361], although the UNEP unintentional POP inventory toolkit contains a dedicated chapter on contaminated sites [311].

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Product life-cycle analysis|Disposal methods_qna_001
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: Are inventories developed for POPs disposed of in landfills within the framework of the Stockholm Convention?
nodes.answer: Inventories of POPs disposed of in landfills or contaminated sites are typically not quantified, with few exceptions such as large pesticide landfills.
nodes.paragraph: Also, many high income countries have disposed POPs containing municipal waste largely in landfills until recently and some coun tries, such as Australia, New Zealand, and the US with limited waste destruction capacity, still dispose POPs containing waste to landfills [46, 167, 184, 189, 362]. Therefore, municipal landfills are joining chemical landfills as reservoirs of POPs and other PBTs albeit at a lower pollution inventory for individual sites, but they represent a large overall inventory considering the hundreds of thousands of landfills including those that predate modern environmental regulations, and which do not have lining and caping systems and waste is not isolated from the surrounding environment [29]. Whilst in the frame of the Stockholm Convention POPs inventories are developed, e.g., for polychlorin ated biphenyls (PCBs) in transformers and capaci tors or PBDEs in electronic waste, the POPs disposed to landfills or in contaminated sites are normally not quantified with some exemptions like large pesticide landfills [234, 294, 349, 351]. Inventories of uninten tionally produced POPs, such as PCDD/PCDF, are largely developed as release inventories for specific years [86, 354] and mostly do not consider the historic reservoirs and releases with a few exemptions [198, 289, 361], although the UNEP unintentional POP inventory toolkit contains a dedicated chapter on contaminated sites [311].

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Product life-cycle analysis|Disposal methods_qna_002
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What was the common method of disposal for chemical production wastes in industrial countries before the 1970s?
nodes.answer: Chemical production wastes, including POPs, were largely landfilled or dumped.
nodes.paragraph: In many industrial countries, chemical produc tion wastes including POPs were largely landfilled or dumped until the 1970s and even 1980s [87, 94, 97, 115, 220, 296, 348, 362, 378]. In low and middle income countries, such production waste is still disposed mostly in dumpsites and landfills due to the limited or absence of destruction capacity [4 , 61, 362, 363]. During the past 60 years brominated, chlorinated and fluorinated POPs and other PBTs have been increas ingly produced [257, 283] and used in consumer goods [39, 40, 112, 121, 273, 316]. An assessment of registered chemicals estimated that approximately 590 of these chemicals are likely POPs considering the Stockholm Convention POP criteria [257]. As products containing these POPs/PBTs reach the end of life, these chemi cals end up in the waste stream [307, 308, 316]. Most low and middle income countries have very limited adequate recycling, treatment, and destruction capac ity, and many countries have relied heavily on landfills and dumps [12, 13, 362, 363].

nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What has been the traditional method of handling SPL?
nodes.answer: The traditional method of handling SPL has been landfilling, as it was the most economically feasible option.
nodes.paragraph: [10]Sommerseth et al. [11]also found NaAISiO 4present in 1st cut SPL. SPL, in reaction with water forms several gases which are important to take into consideration duringpost-treatment of the material as it is a hazardous waste. Ammonia, NH 3, is formed as a reaction between aluminum nitride and water. Phosphorus, which isintroduced together with the alumina raw material inthe form of P 205or AIPO 4,[12]reacts readily with moisture in air and/or water to the poisonous gases called phosphine, PH 3, and sodium cyanide, NaCN, in contact with water forms HCN. Both PH 3and HCN are deadly gases, and hence, SPL must be treated with care. The impurities present make direct reuse di cult, hencepost treatment of the SPL is necessary to transform the waste material into a valuable product. SPL has traditionally been land lled as this has been the most economically feasible method of handling. Ashift in acceptance both socially in terms of environ- mental footprint policies, and an increase in cost for land Il are leading to a need for methods of treating thiswaste to make it usable for new applications.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Product life-cycle analysis|Disposal methods_qna_005
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What commonality is noted among the studies by Schmidt et al. (2004a) and Murphy and Norton (2008)?
nodes.answer: Both studies implemented end-of-life scenario analysis to compare the environmental impacts of products when they are landfilled, incinerated, or composted.
nodes.paragraph: However, Schulte et al. (2021) S work is lim- ited to a point-value result based on a single scenario for transportation, end-of-life and material properties. Schmidt et al. (2004a) implemented the influence of the improvement of manufacturing processes and the consequent impact at the end-of-life scenarios. Nonetheless, also in this case prod- ucts with singularly defined technical performances were investigated. Similarly, Murphy and Norton (2008) investi- gated the environmental impacts of natural fibre insulation materials, using a cradle-to-grave approach. Like Schmidt et al. (2004a) and Murphy and Norton (2008) implemented end-of-life scenario analysis to compare the environmental impacts when products are landfilled, incinerated or com- posted. Also in this case, the study was focused on specific products with defined density and thermal conductivity and did not consider biogenic carbon. There is a clear lack of generalisability for insulation products, when investigating their environmental impacts. Grazieschi et al. (2021) tried to fill the gap in the lit- erature by collecting cradle-to-gate data from Environmen- tal Product Declarations (EPDs) to generate a database of environmental impacts for fossil fuel and bio-based insula- tion materials.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Product life-cycle analysis|Disposal methods_qna_006
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why are products being disposed of quickly and ending up mostly landfilled or incinerated?
nodes.answer: Products are being used for shorter periods of time due to overconsumption culture and poor durability, leading to massive disposals that often end up landfilled or incinerated, particularly in countries with inadequate waste management systems and limited recycling infrastructure.

nodes.answer: It will serve as a starting point for scholars evaluating the sustainability of identified waste management practices.
nodes.paragraph: For practition- ers, this new knowledge adds to the inventory of sustainable waste management practices available to local communi- ties. nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Is it economically viable for companies to comply with waste disposal regulations?
nodes.answer: Sometimes there is a belief that alternative, often illicit methods of waste disposal may generate savings, but not properly disposing of waste can lead to additional costs in the long run.
